findings.documented: Append your API key as a query parameter: GET /v1/listings?api_key=IVY26-XXXXXXXXXXXX
findings.actual: A query-parameter key is rejected with 401 and an explicit error telling you why: {"detail":"send your key in the X-API-Key request header, not as a query parameter"}. The key must be sent as the X-API-Key request header instead.
findings.how_found: Called /v1/listings with api_key as a query parameter and no header, per the documented example.
findings.impact: A client built strictly from the docs cannot authenticate at all.

findings.documented: Response is {token, token_type, expires_in: 86400, user: {email, name}}. Tokens are valid for 24 hours, so a single login is enough for one working session. There is no refresh flow.
findings.actual: Response is {access_token, refresh_token, token_type, expires_in: 900, refresh_url, user: {email}} - the field is access_token not token, there is no user.name, and the token is valid for 15 minutes, not 24 hours.
findings.how_found: Logged in and printed the raw response body before writing any client code around it.
findings.impact: A frontend trusting the documented 24h/no-refresh lifetime would silently stop working 15 minutes after login - which is exactly what this assignment's 'still working thirty minutes after login' requirement tests for.

findings.documented: "There is no refresh flow." No refresh endpoint appears anywhere in the documentation.
findings.actual: POST /auth/refresh exists, takes {refresh_token}, and returns a new {access_token, refresh_token, expires_in} pair - a fully working refresh flow the docs explicitly deny exists.
findings.how_found: The login response itself includes a refresh_url field pointing at /auth/refresh; called it directly with the refresh_token from login.
findings.impact: Anyone following the docs literally would rebuild a full login-and-store-tokens flow every 15 minutes instead of using the working refresh endpoint that's already there.

findings.documented: Every collection endpoint takes page (1-indexed, default 1) and limit. Responses are shaped {total, page, page_size, results}.
findings.actual: Collection endpoints take offset and limit; there is no page parameter at all. Responses are shaped {limit, offset, count, total, has_more, results} - no page or page_size field exists anywhere in the response.
findings.how_found: Called /v1/listings, /v1/rentals and /v1/projects with limit only and inspected the response keys.
findings.impact: The documented pagination recipe (read page_size, increment page) cannot be implemented against the real response shape; you have to page with offset/has_more instead.

findings.actual: The server silently caps limit at 50 regardless of what's requested - passing limit=200 returns a page with "limit": 50 and 50 results, no error.
findings.how_found: Requested /v1/listings?limit=200&offset=0 and read the limit field the server echoed back.
findings.impact: A client that computes total/200 pages up front (per the documented pagination recipe) will under-fetch by 4x; must always trust the echoed limit, not the requested one.

findings.documented: total is the exact number of records matching your filters.
findings.actual: total was stable at 3216 across five consecutive unfiltered calls, both immediately before and immediately after fully paging the same unfiltered endpoint to completion via has_more, which returned 3500 unique, non-duplicated listing_ids.
findings.how_found: Called /v1/listings?limit=1 five times in a row (stable total: 3216), then paged the whole endpoint to completion via has_more (3500 unique ids, no duplicates), then re-checked total again (still 3216).
findings.impact: Following the docs' own advice ("read total, divide by limit, request that many pages") misses roughly 284 real, retrievable records; only driving pagination off has_more retrieves everything.

findings.documented: GET /v1/listing/{listing_id} - A single listing. Same object as above.
findings.actual: 404 {"detail":"Not Found"}. The real path is plural: GET /v1/listings/{listing_id}.
findings.how_found: Requested /v1/listing/100-6000047 (a listing_id returned by /v1/listings) and got a 404; /v1/listings/100-6000047 returns 200.
findings.impact: A listing detail page built from the docs 404s on every listing.

findings.documented: GET /v1/listings/{listing_id}/similar - Up to ten comparable listings.
findings.actual: 404 {"detail":"Not Found"} at that path, and at /v1/listing/{id}/similar as well.
findings.how_found: Requested both plausible paths for a valid listing_id; both 404.
findings.impact: A "you may also like" strip built from the docs has nothing to call.

findings.actual: All three 404. The real resource is /v1/saved: GET /v1/saved, POST /v1/saved with body {"listing_id": ...} (not "id" - posting {"id":...} returns 422 "Field required: listing_id"), and DELETE /v1/saved/{listing_id}.
findings.how_found: Called all three documented favourites endpoints (404), then probed alternative paths until /v1/saved returned 200; confirmed the correct POST body field by reading the 422 validation error.
findings.impact: The saved-listings feature cannot be built at all from the documented path and body shape.

findings.documented: GET /v1/analytics/summary - Pre-computed aggregates for your city.
findings.actual: 404 {"detail":"Not Found"}. No working alternative path was found after probing /v1/analytics, /v1/insights, /v1/insights/summary, /v1/summary, /v1/stats, /v1/dashboard, /v1/metrics, /v1/overview and several other plausible variants - all 404.
findings.how_found: Requested the documented path directly, then systematically probed plausible alternates.
findings.impact: The insights screen cannot be backed by this endpoint at all; it has to be computed client-side from the full listings dataset instead.

findings.documented: price_min and price_max are in rupees. (Conventions table: "Money | Indian rupees, integer, everywhere in the API".)
findings.actual: Values are small decimals on a crore scale (e.g. price_max 98.9, 4.54, 2.15), not integer rupees. Worse, the two fields aren't reliably on the same scale as each other: for 184 of 400 projects, price_min > price_max as reported, which is impossible for a min/max range. In every one of those 184 cases, dividing price_min by 100 (i.e. treating it as lakhs while price_max stays in crores) restores price_min <= price_max. The other 216 projects have both fields already looking like crores (e.g. 1.66/4.54) - but since a project only becomes visibly broken when the two fields land on different scales, there's no way to rule out silent lakhs/crores mixing in that set too.
findings.how_found: Noticed price_max=98.9 for the costliest project (impossible as integer rupees), then compared price_min against price_max across all 400 projects and found 46% were internally inverted, which only resolves by reinterpreting price_min as lakhs.
findings.impact: Any price range shown at face value (including this app's project price display, and the price_max_inr figure required for the costliest_project answer) is wrong for roughly half the city's projects, and can't be trusted as rupees for any of them without a unit conversion.

findings.documented: Returns active sale listings in your city. Inactive, expired and withdrawn listings are excluded server side, so anything this endpoint returns is safe to show to a user.
findings.actual: 708 of 3500 retrievable records have is_live: false - a field that isn't even in the documented Listing object schema. Inactive listings are not excluded; is_live is the only way to tell them apart from live ones.
findings.how_found: Paged the full endpoint and counted is_live values; the field appears on every record despite never being mentioned in the documented Listing object.
findings.impact: Showing every record from this endpoint directly to a user (as the docs say is safe) would surface listings for properties that are no longer actually available.

findings.documented: Every listing_id is globally unique, and each listing corresponds to exactly one physical property.
findings.actual: Cross-referencing listings from different source websites (100acres, zerobroker, magichomes, dwelling, squarelane) by geolocation, project_id, bed/bath/area/price proximity and contact number finds 153 pairs (151 records beyond the first in each group) that describe the same physical property under a different listing_id.
findings.how_found: Built a weighted similarity match (geo distance, project_id, fuzzy name/locality, bed/bath/type, area, price, contact, description) across same-city, different-website record pairs; scored 153 pairs above threshold.
findings.impact: Counting listing records as distinct properties (e.g. for a per-property inventory count) overstates the real number of properties by roughly 4.5%.

findings.documented: Listing object schema (carpet_area, super_built_up_area, floor, total_floors, bedroom, bathroom, price all implied to describe a real, physically possible property).
findings.actual: 18 records describe something that can't exist: carpet_area greater than super_built_up_area, floor greater than total_floors, non-positive price or carpet_area, or a bathroom count implausible relative to bedroom count.
findings.how_found: Checked each retrievable listing against basic physical constraints a real property must satisfy (carpet_area <= super_built_up_area, floor <= total_floors, price > 0, area > 0).
findings.impact: These 18 records can't represent real properties and would need to be excluded from any per-sqft or per-property aggregate to avoid skewing it.

findings.documented: posted_by_contact is the seller's verified contact number.
findings.actual: 230 listing records share a posted_by_contact phone number with other listings posted under a different, unrelated posted_by_name - one 'verified' phone number claimed by multiple distinct people, consistent with listings created to generate enquiries rather than genuine ones.
findings.how_found: Grouped listings by posted_by_contact and flagged any group whose posted_by_name values don't reduce to the same person (normalized, token-sorted name comparison).
findings.impact: These listings shouldn't be treated as genuine seller-backed inventory; including them in seller-facing or trust-sensitive views would be misleading.

findings.documented: total_listings is the number of listings currently available in the project. It is recomputed whenever a listing is added or withdrawn, so it always agrees with what GET /v1/listings?project_id=... returns.
findings.actual: For 106 of 400 projects, total_listings does not match the count of that project's live listings from /v1/listings. A large share are reported as 0 while live listings actually exist (e.g. P60011 reports 0, has 9).
findings.how_found: Counted live listings per project_id from the full /v1/listings pull and compared against each project's total_listings.
findings.impact: total_listings can't be trusted as a live inventory count for over a quarter of projects; a project page showing 0 listings may actually have several available.

findings.actual: order has no effect. Tested sort_by=price, carpet_area, posted_at and bedroom, each with order=asc and order=desc: every pair returned byte-identical result sets, always in ascending order. Omitting order entirely also matches order=asc.
findings.how_found: Called the same sort_by with order=asc and order=desc back to back and diffed the results, across four different sort_by fields.
findings.impact: There is no way to get a descending sort (e.g. "most expensive first") from this endpoint; a UI sort-direction toggle has nothing to bind to server-side.

findings.documented: total_listings ... always agrees with what GET /v1/listings?project_id=... returns (implying project_id is a working filter, even though it's absent from the documented query parameter table).
findings.actual: project_id is silently ignored: /v1/listings?project_id=P60001 returns the same total (3216) as no filter at all, with results spanning many different project_ids (and null).
findings.how_found: Filtered by a known valid project_id and compared the total and returned project_id values against an unfiltered call.
findings.impact: The docs' own claim that total_listings can be verified via this filter is unverifiable in practice - the filter that claim depends on doesn't work.

findings.documented: Invalidates the current token server side.
findings.actual: Returns 200 {"ok":true,"note":"tokens are stateless; discard them client side"}. The same access token continues to authenticate requests successfully after logout - it is never actually invalidated server side.
findings.how_found: Called /auth/logout, then immediately reused the same (pre-logout) access token against /v1/listings and got a normal 200 response.
findings.impact: A logged-out session's token remains valid for the rest of its 15-minute lifetime; "logout" is a client-side-only convention, not a real server-side revocation.
